  A monitoring, veriﬁcation, and accounting (MVA) plan
is a critical component of a CCS project and has a number
of objectives including managing of MVA-related project
risks, establishing baseline conditions, demonstrating that
project activities are protective of human health and the en-
vironment, and providing accurate accounting of stored CO2
(Locke et al., 2013). Beginning long before injection com-
menced, extensive  site characterization eﬀorts have taken
place at the IBDP site that has included 2D and 3D surface
seismic surveys as well as well logging and coring programs in
the injection (CCS1) and veriﬁcation (VW1) well (Figure 1).

Mt. Simon sandstone has average interval porosities of 20%
and permeability of 185 mD and is the storage target for
IBDP; however, there are low permeability units within the
lower Mt. Simon Sandstone with permeabilities <1 mD that
act as baﬄes to upward CO2 migration (Finley et al., 2013).
   The primary seal for the Mt. Simon sandstone is the re-
gionally extensive Eau Claire shale, which is approximately
500-ft thick at the site and primarily composed of black ma-
rine shale, silty mudstones, low-permeability siltstones, and
carbonates (Finley et al., 2013). The Mt. Simon sandstone
is underlain by a thin Pre-Mt. Simon sandstone unit as well
as granitic or rhyolitic Precambrian basement (Leetaru and
McBride, 2009).

acquisition and imaging. Surface features such as housing, a
community college, major industrial sites, railroads, power
distribution facilities, and municipal public works infrastruc-
ture presented major challenges in the form of noise contami-
nation, electrical interference, and obstructed access. These
factors impact the quality of the time-lapse 3D VSP data
that is acquired in regards to acquisition footprint and non-
repeated time-lapse noise. Over time, the footprint of the 3D
VSP surveys has been further reduced through lack of access
to adjacent properties (Figure 4).
     Initially, the project plan was to acquire the baseline 3D
VSP survey simultaneously with the 3D surface seismic data
without adding additional shot points (Couëslan et al., 2008).
However, survey design and modeling showed that the shot
and shot-line spacing of the 3D surface seismic survey was
too sparse to provide adequate 3D VSP images at the site.
Since 2010, two baseline 3D VSPs and two monitor 3D VSP
surveys have been acquired at IBDP (Table 1). Baseline 1
(B1) was acquired in February 2010 when the ground condi-
tions were deteriorating as the frost started to melt, and there
were also signiﬁcant amounts of 60-Hz noise from electrical
sources in the data. In the spring of 2011, a new baseline
(B2) 3D VSP survey was acquired after work had been com-
pleted on the surface-based geophone array electronics that
decreased the amount of 60-Hz noise recorded by the array.
In addition, ground conditions for the B2 survey were dry,
which further improved data quality.
   In 2012, the ﬁrst monitor 3D VSP survey (M1) was ac-
quired after ~70,000 tons of CO2 had been injected, which is
a relatively small volume of CO2 to detect seismically. How-
ever, the ﬁrst monitor survey was timed to coincide with the
ﬁrst round of time-lapse RST logging in CCS1 and VW1 as
well as the deep ﬂuid sampling in VW1. The Monitor 2 3D
VSP survey (M2) was acquired in April 2013 when 433,000
tons of CO2 had been injected. Ground conditions were not
as optimal as B2 and M1 because of a late snowfall and damp
weather. In addition, because of inaccessibility, 77 shot points
were lost on the east side of the survey.

    Pressure measurements from VW1 further support the
fact that the CO2 is conﬁned below 6837 ft. Pressures mea-
sured at Westbay sampling ports 2 and 3, at 6982 and 6945
ft, respectively, respond quickly to injection operations.
However, the pressures at Westbay sampling port 4 (6837
ft) have shown only a small and gradual increase over time
indicating that the CO2 plume has not migrated to this
depth. A low-permeability zone in the lower Mt. Simon
sandstone is known to exist between sampling ports 3 and
4 based on the well-log data, and it appears to be blocking
pressure and ﬂuid transmission at this time.

Discussion
The nrms repeatability metrics through the injection in-
terval show stable anomalies, which are indicative of CO2
plume development between the B2, M1, and M2 3D VSP
surveys. However, more work is required to support the in-
terpretation of these observations. The time-lapse seismic
response in rock/ﬂuid systems is a complex combination of
rock and ﬂuid properties that change over time and space.
This can cause ambiguity in the direct interpretation of
the seismic data on a stand-alone basis. This complexity
increases in CO2-brine systems where additional processes
such as phase transitions, dehydration, and changes to the
rock matrix may occur through mineral dissolution and
precipitation. Some of these ambiguities may be signiﬁ-
cantly reduced through the addition of rock physics and
ﬂuid substitution modeling to the interpretation work-
ﬂow. Rock physics modeling has been performed using the
log data from the IBDP wells; however, the ﬂuid substitu-
tion modeling will be revisited using the new pressure and
saturation predictions derived from the latest calibrated
reservoir simulation model. Pending the results of the new
ﬂuid substitution modeling, the interpretation of the time-
lapse seismic response may be used to update the spatial
plume predictions from the reservoir model in regions
lacking direct MVA measurements.
   Based on the results of the M2 survey, IBDP will likely
proceed with a third monitor survey in 2014 near the end
of injection because the project may be required to dem-
onstrate that the bulk of the CO2 plume can be identiﬁed
through MVA data. The results of the IBDP time-lapse 3D
VSPs will also be used to help inform the MVA plan that
is being developed for the adjacent Illinois Industrial CCS
Project (ICCS). While the Illinois ICCS Project plans to
inject higher volumes of CO2, time-lapse 3D VSPs will
likely still play a large role in monitoring CO2 plume de-
velopment over the life of that project as well.
